About: Single-Slit Diffraction

Source

Topic
Wave optics — single-slit diffraction (Class 12)
Concept
Narrowing the slit makes the diffraction pattern WIDER — squeeze a wave in space and it spreads in angle.
Standard result
First minimum at a·sinθ = λ; central band width on a screen at distance L is 2λL/a.
Misconception
"The pattern is the shadow of the slit" — exactly backwards; the central band width goes as 1/a.

Guided Inquiry

The starting picture

Light of wavelength 550 nm hits a slit of width a = 100 µm. The central bright band is 11 mm wide.

You are about to halve the slit to 50 µm. What happens to the central band?

Now do it

Drag the Slit width a slider down from 100 µm to 50 µm and watch the central band. Notice the screen scale doesn't move — the pattern really does grow.

Read the central band width readout as you drag. It should reach about 22 mm at a = 50 µm.

Why? The first minimum

At the first dark fringe, light from one edge of the slit arrives one wavelength behind light from the other edge. Split the slit in two: every point in the top half has a partner in the bottom half exactly λ/2 behind it, so the pairs cancel and the slit goes dark. Hence a·sinθ = λ, and sinθ = λ/a.

Smaller a ⇒ larger θ ⇒ wider central band: W = 2λL/a on a screen at distance L, so the spread goes as 1/a.

And the wavelength?

Try dragging Wavelength λ from 550 nm (green) toward 700 nm (deep red). The central band grows again — longer waves spread more, because sinθ = λ/a.

The faint bumps outside the central band are side lobes. The first one reaches only about 4.7% of the central peak — the dark bands really are dark.

The one thing to notice

Narrowing the slit makes the pattern wider. Confine a wave in space and it must spread in angle — the tighter you squeeze, the more it fans out. It is not a shadow of the slit; it is diffraction.

Play freely with both sliders. The screen scale stays fixed at ±25 mm so the growth stays visible.

Single-Slit Diffraction

✦Learn this with the AI tutor

01

At a glance

A wave that meets a barrier with a narrow slit does not just continue as a thin beam. This sim sends light through one slit onto a screen 1.00 m away and shows the pattern of bright and dark bands that lands there.

What you'll learn

  • Why light that passes through a slit makes a pattern of bright and dark bands.
  • Where the first dark band lands, and what fixes its position.
  • How the brightness is shared out across the screen.
The apparatus. A plane wave meets a slit of width a. The angle θ is measured from the straight-ahead line.

What's on screen

  • Barrier and slit: the dark bar at the left with a gap, labelled with the width a.
  • Intensity curve: the brightness I/I₀ plotted against the position y on the screen, in mm.
  • Dashed pink lines: the first dark fringes, marked m = 1, with the width W of the band between them.

The strip above the curve shows the same pattern as light on the screen. The slit is drawn far wider than the real one, and the sim says so: schematic, not to scale.

See itUse the opening setup, a = 100 µm and λ = 550 nm. Watch for: vertical wave lines at the left, a slit in the dark bar, and a bright band in the middle of the strip on the right.

03

Every point of the slit sends out its own wavelet

Light is a wave. Each point in the opening of the slit acts as a source of a small circular wavelet, and all of them start in step because they come from the same plane wave. Those are the arcs leaving the slit in the sim.

At a point on the screen the wavelets arrive from different distances, so they arrive with different phases and add. Where they arrive in step, the screen is bright. Where they cancel, it is dark. The whole pattern is this sum.

  • The screen is far away compared with the slit, so the rays reaching one point are almost parallel. A single angle θ from the straight-ahead line describes that point, with y = L tan θ.
  • Straight ahead every wavelet travels the same distance, so they add in step. The centre of the screen is bright.
  • The central bright band ends at the first dark fringe on each side. Its full width is W.
See itLook at the slit itself. Watch for: circular arcs spreading to the right of the slit, from several points along its gap.
04

The first dark fringe is where the two halves of the slit cancel

Pick the direction in which light from the top edge of the slit arrives exactly one wavelength behind light from the bottom edge. The path difference between the edges is a sin θ, so this direction has a sin θ = λ.

Now split the slit into two halves. Every point in the upper half has a partner a/2 below it, and the partner's wavelet is behind by (a/2) sin θ = λ/2. That is exactly out of step, so each pair cancels and the whole slit gives darkness.

a sin θ = mλ    m = ±1, ±2, …
Dark fringes. Splitting the slit into 2m parts gives the higher orders.
  • At the opening values sin θ = λ/a = 550 nm / 100 µm = 0.0055, so θ = 0.315°.
  • The equation looks like the double-slit one for bright fringes. For a single slit it marks the dark ones, and m = 0 is left out because straight ahead is bright.
See itRead the first dark fringe at the opening setup. Watch for: First minimum θ = 0.315° in the readouts, and the dashed pink lines marked m = 1 at about ±5.5 mm on the axis.
05

A narrower slit gives a wider central band

Since sin θ = λ/a, a smaller a gives a larger θ. On the screen y = L tan θ, and for these small angles tan θ ≈ sin θ, so the first minimum sits at y = λL/a on each side of the centre. The full width between them is:

W = 2λL/a
Small-angle form. The sim's readout uses the exact angle.
  • At a = 100 µm, W = 2 × 550 nm × 1.00 m / 100 µm = 11.0 mm. Halving the slit to 50 µm doubles it to 22.0 mm, and θ doubles to 0.630°.
  • At a = 25 µm the band is 44.0 mm wide. At a = 300 µm it shrinks to 3.67 mm.
  • The pattern is not the shadow of the slit. A shadow would shrink with the slit. The band grows, and at a = 100 µm it is 110 times wider than the slit.

A wave squeezed into a narrow space spreads out in angle.

See itHalve the slit to a = 50 µm. Watch for: Central band width 22.00 mm in the readouts, the dashed m = 1 lines at about ±11 mm, and the gap in the dark bar closing.
06

A longer wavelength gives a wider central band

W = 2λL/a is proportional to λ. The first minimum needs a path difference of one wavelength between the edges, and a longer wavelength needs a larger angle to reach it. Only the ratio λ/a sets the angle.

  • At a = 100 µm, λ = 400 nm gives W = 8.00 mm, 550 nm gives 11.00 mm and 700 nm gives 14.00 mm.
  • The slit is always much wider than the light. The narrowest slit, 25 µm, is about 36 times the longest wavelength, so a first minimum always exists.
  • At a = 25 µm the first minima fall beyond the ±25 mm screen once λ passes about 625 nm. The sim then writes first minima → off screen and draws no dashed lines. At 700 nm they would be at ±28.0 mm.
See itRaise the wavelength to λ = 700 nm. Watch for: Central band width 14.00 mm in the readouts, the dashed lines at about ±7 mm, and the strip shifting toward red.
07

The side lobes are far fainter than the central band

Adding all the wavelets gives the intensity:

I = I0 (sin β / β)²    β = π a sin θ / λ
The same sinc² shape the sim draws as the teal curve.
  • β = 0 is the centre. The zeros fall at β = mπ, which is a sin θ = mλ again.
  • Between zeros there are small bumps, the side lobes. The first peaks at β ≈ 4.49, where I/I₀ = 0.0472, about 4.7% of the central peak. At the opening setup it sits near y = 7.87 mm.
  • Every band outside the centre is half as wide as the central one: at the opening setup 5.50 mm against 11.0 mm.

The curve is to scale. The strip is brightened a little so the faint bands show, so trust the curve for heights.

See itCompare the side bumps with the centre. Watch for: small teal bumps between the m = 1 lines and the ticks at ±11 mm, each only a few percent of the central height.
08

The brightness straight ahead goes as the square of the slit width

Straight ahead every point of the slit adds in step, so the amplitude is proportional to a and the intensity I₀ is proportional to a². The strip and the curve are each scaled to their own peak, so the readout Brightness I₀ ∝ a² carries this, measured against a = 100 µm.

  • a = 50 µm gives 0.25×, a = 200 µm gives 4.00× and a = 300 µm gives 9.00×.
  • This agrees with the width. The light let through is proportional to a. Spread over a band that goes as 1/a, the peak goes as a × a.

A narrower slit lets through less light, and spreads it wider, so the centre dims faster than the slit shrinks.

See itWiden the slit to a = 300 µm. Watch for: Brightness 9.00× and Central band width 3.67 mm in the readouts, with a narrow central band on the strip.
09

Summary

In one line. Light passing through a slit spreads out, and the pattern on the screen is the sum of the wavelets from every point of the opening.

Key points

  • Dark fringes at a sin θ = mλ, with m = ±1, ±2, … and never m = 0.
  • The central band has full width W = 2λL/a, so W ∝ λ/a. The side lobes are far fainter: the first is about 4.7% of the peak.
  • The central brightness I₀ ∝ a².

Common mix-ups

  • "The pattern is the shadow of the slit." A narrower slit gives a wider pattern.
  • "a sin θ = mλ marks the bright fringes." For a single slit it marks the dark ones.

Things to try on your own

  • Set λ = 400 nm and a = 25 µm, and read W. It is 32.0 mm.
  • Double a from 100 to 200 µm and check that W halves to 5.50 mm.
